title: Addressing modes
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Find the operand or effective address from registers and instruction fields.
theory: Immediate embeds the operand; direct uses the address field; indirect follows a memory pointer.
Register indirect uses a register as an address. Base/index/PC-relative add a displacement to the specified register.

recall.q: Does memory-indirect addressing need more memory accesses than direct addressing?
recall.a: Normally one additional access to fetch the effective address, excluding instruction fetch.

pitfall: Use the stated PC value and instruction length; do not assume whether PC was already advanced.

title: Average memory access time
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: A hit ratio and several access times appear.
theory: For serial cache lookup: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × additional miss penalty.
For multiple levels, expand the miss penalty recursively using each level's local miss rate.

recall.q: When is h×tcache + (1−h)×tmemory wrong?
recall.a: When tmemory omits the cache lookup already spent on a miss; count the complete path times.

pitfall: A miss penalty can already include lookup time; check its definition before adding it again.

title: Bit vectors and storage overhead
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: One status bit is maintained for every block or page.
theory: One bit per N objects needs N bits, or ceil(N/8) bytes.
For memory allocation maps, number of bits = managed capacity / allocation-unit size, rounded up.

recall.q: How many bytes store one status bit for 1,024 blocks?
recall.a: 128 bytes.

pitfall: Do not confuse bits of metadata with bytes of data.

title: CISC and RISC
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Compare instruction formats, addressing and control choices.
theory: RISC commonly emphasizes simple operations and load/store access; CISC commonly offers richer instruction forms.
These are design tendencies; performance still depends on instruction count, CPI and clock period.

recall.q: Is lower instruction count alone proof of faster execution?
recall.a: No. Compare instruction count × CPI × cycle time.

pitfall: Avoid absolute claims that every RISC instruction is one cycle or every CISC design is microprogrammed.

title: Cache organization and policies
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: An address trace, block size, cache capacity or hit rate is given.
theory: Number of lines = cache data capacity / block size; sets = lines / associativity.
For power-of-two, byte-addressed layouts: offset bits = log₂(block bytes), index bits = log₂(sets), tag bits = address bits − index − offset.
Write-through updates lower memory on each write; write-back writes dirty blocks when evicted.

recall.q: What part of an address selects a byte within a cache block?
recall.a: The block-offset bits.

pitfall: Do not include metadata in the stated data capacity unless the question explicitly does.

title: Conflict misses
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Different memory blocks repeatedly evict one another.
theory: Conflict misses arise from placement restrictions and would disappear in a fully associative cache of the same capacity with a comparable policy.
Blocks mapping to the same set compete for its available ways.

recall.q: Can a fully associative cache have conflict misses under the usual 3C classification?
recall.a: No; compulsory and capacity misses can remain.

pitfall: A first reference to a block is compulsory, even if it also maps to a crowded set.

title: Control-unit design
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Determine the signals that execute a machine operation.
theory: The control unit sequences register transfers, ALU operations and memory actions.
Hardwired control derives signals from logic; microprogrammed control reads control words from a control store.

recall.q: What distinguishes hardwired from microprogrammed control?
recall.a: Combinational/sequential logic generates signals versus stored microinstructions sequencing them.

pitfall: The control store is distinct from the program's main memory.

title: Direct memory access
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: A device transfers a stream while stealing bus cycles.
theory: DMA moves blocks between a device and memory with limited CPU intervention.
Stolen cycles per second = transfers per second × bus cycles per transfer; fraction of available cycles stolen is that value divided by available cycles per second.

recall.q: A device sends 1,200 bytes/s and one DMA transfer moves 2 bytes. How many transfers/s?
recall.a: 600 transfers/s if bytes can be packed in pairs.

pitfall: Instructions per second are not automatically bus cycles per second; use the question's stated timing model.

title: DRAM organization
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Memory chips, row/column selection or refresh are described.
theory: DRAM stores charge and requires refresh; SRAM uses bistable storage and does not require periodic refresh.
With multiplexed addresses, row and column address bits may share physical pins.

recall.q: Why can a DRAM chip have fewer address pins than address bits?
recall.a: Row and column addresses are supplied in separate phases through shared pins.

pitfall: Do not count shared address pins twice; distinguish chip width from number of locations.

title: Data dependencies
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Instructions read and write common registers.
theory: RAW is a true dependence: a later instruction needs an earlier result.
WAR and WAW are name dependencies; renaming can remove these but cannot remove the underlying RAW value requirement.

recall.q: Which dependencies can register renaming remove?
recall.a: WAR and WAW name dependencies.

pitfall: A dependency is a program property; whether it causes a stall depends on the pipeline.

title: Data hazards and forwarding
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Find stalls between dependent instructions.
theory: A RAW hazard occurs when a consumer needs a value before the pipeline can supply it.
Forwarding may supply a result before writeback, but a load-use pair can still need a stall depending on stages.

recall.q: Does forwarding guarantee zero data stalls?
recall.a: No. The result must exist by the consumer's required stage.

pitfall: Draw a stage timeline; do not use a fixed stall count without the given architecture.

title: Datapath and ALU
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Trace registers, buses, multiplexers and arithmetic operations.
theory: A datapath moves operands between registers, ALU and memory under control signals.
On a single shared bus, transfers that compete for the bus cannot occur simultaneously; independent internal operations may overlap.

recall.q: What determines whether two register transfers fit in one cycle?
recall.a: Available buses, ports and functional units, plus control/timing constraints.

pitfall: Count actual resource conflicts, not merely the number of written micro-operations.

title: Direct-mapped cache
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Each memory block has exactly one possible cache line.
theory: Cache line index = memory block number mod number of lines.
Tag = floor(memory block number / number of lines); byte offset identifies a byte within the block.

recall.q: Which blocks conflict in a direct-mapped cache with L lines?
recall.a: Blocks whose numbers have the same remainder modulo L.

pitfall: Compute the block number from the address before taking the modulus.

title: Disk access time
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Seek, RPM, sector size and transfer size are given.
theory: Disk access time combines seek, rotational latency and transfer, plus any stated overhead.
One rotation takes 60/RPM seconds; average random rotational latency is half a rotation.

recall.q: At 7,200 RPM, what is the average rotational latency?
recall.a: About 4.167 ms.

pitfall: Transfer time is for the requested data; it is not automatically a complete rotation.

title: Pipeline hazards
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: A pipeline stalls because an instruction cannot proceed.
theory: Structural hazards are resource conflicts; data hazards involve values; control hazards involve the next instruction address.
A branch penalty affects only the branch events specified by the model.

recall.q: What is a structural hazard?
recall.a: Two overlapping instructions need a resource that cannot serve both at once.

pitfall: A register dependence and an actual timing hazard are different concepts.

title: Programmed and interrupt-driven I/O
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Compare busy waiting, interrupts and DMA.
theory: Programmed I/O polls device status and transfers data through the CPU.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until notified; DMA can transfer blocks without CPU instructions for each word.

recall.q: Which method avoids CPU data-transfer instructions for every word?
recall.a: DMA.

pitfall: Interrupt overhead and CPU transfer overhead are separate quantities.

title: Instruction execution and timing
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Find execution time from instruction classes or machine cycles.
theory: CPU time = instruction count × average CPI × clock period.
Weighted CPI = Σ(fraction of instructions in class i × CPIᵢ).

recall.q: What changes if instruction count falls but CPI rises?
recall.a: Recompute the product; either effect can dominate.

pitfall: Use instruction fractions for CPI, not fractions of total time.

title: Instruction formats and encoding
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Opcode, register and address fields must fit in a word.
theory: Selecting R registers takes ceil(log₂R) bits per register field.
The remaining instruction bits limit opcode or address possibilities; variable-length opcode schemes require prefix-compatible encodings.

recall.q: How many bits select one of 32 registers?

pitfall: Do not assume all unused bit patterns are independent opcodes in an expanding-opcode scheme.

title: Instruction set architecture
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Separate programmer-visible behavior from implementation.
theory: The ISA defines operations, registers, data types and addressing visible to machine-code programmers.
Different microarchitectures can implement the same ISA with different pipelines and performance.

recall.q: Can two CPUs share an ISA but use different pipelines?
recall.a: Yes.

pitfall: A cache size or pipeline depth is usually a microarchitectural detail, not an ISA requirement.

title: Interrupts
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: A device or exception diverts control to a handler.
theory: An interrupt saves sufficient execution state and transfers control to an appropriate handler.
Priority and masking rules determine which pending interrupt can be serviced; nesting requires suitable saved state.

recall.q: Why save the program counter on an interrupt?
recall.a: So interrupted execution can resume at the architecturally defined return point.

pitfall: Do not equate every interrupt with a process switch.

title: Machine instructions and register transfers
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Execute a short assembly fragment or count machine operations.
theory: Track each instruction's source values, destination, flags and next PC in order.
Distinguish instruction fetch, operand accesses and result writes when counting memory traffic.

recall.q: What is the safest way to trace machine code?
recall.a: Keep a table of PC, registers and relevant memory after each instruction.

pitfall: An instruction that references memory can cause more than one memory access.

title: Memory-chip interfacing
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Build a target memory from smaller chips.
theory: Chips in parallel increase word width; banks increase the number of addressable words.
Total chips = (target words / chip words) × (target word width / chip width), for exact integer dimensions.

recall.q: How many 1K×4 chips make 2K×8 memory?
recall.a: 4 chips: two in parallel per bank and two banks.

pitfall: Byte-addressable capacity and word-addressable capacity give different address-bit counts.

title: Microprogrammed control
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Control memory contains microinstructions and next-address fields.
theory: A microinstruction selects control signals and how the next microaddress is obtained.
Horizontal encoding exposes many control bits; vertical encoding compresses signals and needs decoding.

recall.q: What is the usual tradeoff of vertical microcode?
recall.a: Fewer stored bits, with decoding and potentially less parallel control.

pitfall: Mutually exclusive signals can share an encoded field; simultaneous signals may need separate fields.

title: Pipeline timing
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Compute total time for several instructions through stages.
theory: Ideal time for n instructions in a k-stage pipeline is (k+n−1)×cycle time.
Cycle time is usually the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead; add specified stall cycles.

recall.q: Does pipelining mainly reduce one instruction's latency or improve throughput?
recall.a: Throughput; individual latency may stay similar or increase.

pitfall: For a short stream, include fill and drain time instead of assuming speedup = k.

title: Runtime stack and procedure calls
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: A call changes stack frames, return addresses and saved registers.
theory: A stack frame holds the activation's parameters, locals and saved state according to a calling convention.
Recursion requires distinct live activation records even for the same procedure.

recall.q: Why does recursion need multiple activation records?
recall.a: Each active call has its own locals and return information.

pitfall: Do not assume stack growth direction or parameter layout unless specified.

title: Speedup and Amdahl's law
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Only a fraction of the original execution is improved.
theory: Speedup = old time / new time.
If fraction f of original time is accelerated by factor s, overall speedup = 1 / ((1−f)+f/s).

recall.q: What is the limit as s approaches infinity?
recall.a: 1/(1−f), provided f<1.

pitfall: f is a fraction of original execution time, not necessarily an instruction-count fraction.

title: Stalls and effective CPI
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Branch frequency or hazard frequency adds cycles.
theory: Effective CPI = base CPI + Σ(event frequency per instruction × penalty cycles).
CPU time still includes clock period; reduced CPI does not guarantee speedup if the clock slows.

recall.q: With base CPI 1 and 20% branches each costing 2 extra cycles, what is CPI?

pitfall: If only mispredictions stall, multiply branch frequency by misprediction probability first.

title: Virtual memory and translation
subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
cue: Virtual addresses, TLBs and page walks appear in a COA problem.
theory: Split a virtual address into page number and unchanged page offset.
A TLB caches translations; a TLB miss triggers a page-table lookup, which need not be a page fault.

recall.q: Is every TLB miss a page fault?
recall.a: No. The page may be resident and only its translation absent from the TLB.

pitfall: Count translation and data accesses according to the stated cache/TLB organization.

title: Application-layer protocols
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Match a service to DNS, HTTP, mail or file transfer.
theory: DNS resolves names and other resource records; HTTP defines web request/response semantics.
For classic GATE problems: SMTP transfers mail, FTP transfers files, and DNS can use UDP or TCP depending on the operation.

recall.q: Is DNS restricted to UDP?
recall.a: No; DNS uses both UDP and TCP.

pitfall: Do not infer the transport solely from the application's name when the question specifies a version or operation.

title: ARP
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A host knows an IPv4 next-hop address but needs its link-layer address.
theory: ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a link-layer address on a local link.
For a remote destination, the host normally resolves its gateway's link-layer address, not the remote host's.

recall.q: Which MAC address is used when sending to an off-subnet host?
recall.a: The next-hop router's MAC address on the local link.

pitfall: IP destination remains the remote host while the Ethernet destination is the next hop.

title: Bit stuffing
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A frame delimiter must not appear in transmitted data.
theory: In the usual HDLC rule, the sender inserts a 0 after five consecutive data 1s.
The receiver removes stuffed zeros; stuffing is applied to frame contents, not by altering the delimiter itself.

recall.q: What happens after five consecutive 1s in HDLC data?
recall.a: Insert a 0.

pitfall: Count consecutive bits in the transmitted stream according to the rule; restart the run after the inserted zero.

title: Bridges and learning switches
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A switch learns addresses or forwards unknown destinations.
theory: A learning bridge records source MAC addresses with their incoming ports.
Known destinations are forwarded selectively; unknown destinations are flooded on other eligible ports.

recall.q: Does a switch learn from source or destination addresses?
recall.a: Source addresses of received frames.

pitfall: Learning and forwarding are separate steps; exclude the incoming port from flooding.

title: CRC polynomial arithmetic
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Generator polynomial or an error polynomial is given.
theory: CRC divides M(x)xʳ by a degree-r generator using arithmetic over GF(2); the remainder supplies r check bits.
An error is undetected exactly when its error polynomial is divisible by the generator.

recall.q: What replaces subtraction in CRC long division?
recall.a: XOR.

pitfall: Ordinary integer subtraction and carrying do not apply to GF(2) polynomial division.

title: CSMA/CD
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Find minimum frame size, collision timing or cable length.
theory: To detect a worst-case collision while still transmitting, frame transmission time must be at least the round-trip propagation time.
Thus minimum frame bits ≥ 2×one-way propagation delay×bit rate under the simple model.

recall.q: What timing inequality gives the minimum frame length?
recall.a: L/R ≥ 2d/v.

pitfall: CSMA/CD applies to shared half-duplex Ethernet, not ordinary switched full-duplex links.

title: Channel utilization
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Frame size, link rate and round-trip waiting time are given.
theory: For error-free stop-and-wait with negligible ACK transmission, utilization = Ttx/(Ttx+2Tprop).
Throughput = utilization × link rate under that model.

recall.q: Why does a fast long-distance link have poor stop-and-wait utilization?
recall.a: The sender waits a long propagation round trip after a short transmission.

pitfall: Convert milliseconds and bits consistently before forming the ratio.

title: End-to-end communication delay
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A message crosses one or several links.
theory: Transmission delay = bits / link rate; propagation delay = distance / signal speed.
Store-and-forward switches receive a whole packet before forwarding; multiple packets may then pipeline across links.

recall.q: Which delay increases with message size on a fixed link?
recall.a: Transmission delay.

pitfall: Do not multiply the complete file's transmission time by every hop when packets are pipelined.

title: TCP congestion control
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A congestion window changes after ACKs or losses.
theory: Classic slow start grows the window approximately exponentially by RTT; congestion avoidance grows approximately linearly.
Loss response depends on the stated TCP variant and whether loss is detected by timeout or duplicate ACKs.

recall.q: Which two limits constrain outstanding TCP data?
recall.a: Congestion window and receiver-advertised window.

pitfall: Do not use Tahoe, Reno and newer variant rules interchangeably.

title: Data communication and link capacity
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Distinguish bit rate, symbol rate and delivery time.
theory: Bit rate measures transmitted bits per second; symbol rate measures signalling events per second.
With M distinct symbols carrying fixed-length labels, each symbol represents log₂M bits when M is a power of two.

recall.q: Is 1,000 baud necessarily 1,000 bit/s?
recall.a: No; multiple bits may be encoded in one symbol.

pitfall: Bandwidth in hertz and data rate in bits/s are different quantities.

title: Distance-vector routing
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Routers exchange distance tables with neighbors.
theory: Bellman-Ford update: Dₓ(y) = minᵥ[c(x,v)+Dᵥ(y)] over neighbors v.
Each router combines its direct link costs with neighbors' advertised costs.

recall.q: What local information does a distance-vector router use?
recall.a: Its neighbor link costs and neighbors' distance estimates.

pitfall: Updates can propagate over several rounds; do not instantly give every router global information.

title: Error detection
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Parity, checksum, CRC or minimum distance is specified.
theory: A code with minimum Hamming distance d detects every error pattern of up to d−1 bits.
It can correct every pattern of up to floor((d−1)/2) bit errors.

recall.q: What minimum distance guarantees detection of every two-bit error?

pitfall: Detecting an error and locating it for correction require different redundancy.

title: Ethernet
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Frames, MAC addresses, collision domains or switching appear.
theory: Ethernet is a link-layer frame technology using MAC addresses.
A switch separates collision domains; routers separate IP subnets and usually broadcast domains.

recall.q: Does a router forward an Ethernet frame unchanged across different links?
recall.a: No; it forwards the IP packet using a new link-layer encapsulation.

pitfall: Do not apply shared-medium collisions to a full-duplex point-to-point Ethernet link.

title: IPv4 fragmentation
subject: Computer Networks
cue: An IP packet exceeds an outgoing link's MTU.
theory: Maximum nonfinal fragment payload is 8×floor((MTU−header bytes)/8).
Fragment offsets are in units of 8 bytes relative to the original IP payload; each fragment carries its own IP header.

recall.q: Why round most fragment payloads down to a multiple of eight?
recall.a: The next fragment's offset must be expressed in 8-byte units.

pitfall: MTU includes the IP header; the final fragment need not have an 8-byte-multiple payload.

title: Hamming code and syndrome
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Parity checks identify a flipped bit.
theory: Place parity bits at positions 1,2,4,8,…; parity bit 2ᵏ checks positions whose binary index has bit k set.
For standard single-error-correcting Hamming code, a nonzero syndrome gives the erroneous position, including a parity-bit position.

recall.q: What if the syndrome equals 4?
recall.a: Flip bit position 4 under the single-bit-error assumption; it is a parity bit.

pitfall: Ordinary Hamming code cannot safely correct arbitrary double-bit errors; extended parity changes the detection capability.

title: IPv4 addressing and CIDR
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A prefix length identifies a network block.
theory: An IPv4 /p prefix contains 2^(32−p) addresses; network address is IP bitwise-AND mask.
Classless routing uses the prefix length, not an assumed address class.

NAT rewrites IP addresses at a boundary; port translation can also rewrite transport ports so several internal hosts share an external address. Keep internal and external address/port mappings distinct.

recall.q: How many total addresses are in a /26 block?

pitfall: The familiar hosts = addresses−2 rule has exceptions, notably /31 point-to-point and /32 routes.

title: IPv4 packet fields
subject: Computer Networks
cue: TTL, header length, total length or checksum changes.
theory: IPv4 total length includes header and payload; IHL counts 32-bit words.
TTL is decremented by routers; the IPv4 header checksum covers the header, not the payload.

recall.q: An IHL of 5 means how many header bytes?
recall.a: 20 bytes.

pitfall: TCP/UDP payload sizes differ from IP total length because protocol headers must be removed.

title: ICMP
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A network reports unreachable destinations or expired packets.
theory: ICMP carries control and error reports for IP, including destination unreachable and time exceeded.
Ping commonly uses ICMP echo messages; ICMP is carried in IP.

recall.q: What normally reports a TTL expiration?
recall.a: ICMP Time Exceeded.

pitfall: ICMP is not a reliable application-data transport protocol.

title: LAN technologies
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Compare LAN topology, access method and forwarding devices.
theory: A hub repeats physical signals, a bridge switches link-layer frames, and a router forwards network-layer packets.
The shared or switched topology determines contention and forwarding behavior.

recall.q: Which device normally uses IP prefixes to forward packets?
recall.a: A router.

pitfall: A physical star topology can still represent a logically shared medium when a hub is used.

title: Medium-access protocols
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Several senders contend or take assigned slots.
theory: Random access resolves competing transmissions probabilistically; TDMA assigns time slots and token schemes grant turns.
For n independent senders each transmitting with probability p in a slot, success probability = np(1−p)^(n−1).

recall.q: What is one station's probability of a successful transmission in that slot?

pitfall: Separate one station's throughput from aggregate network throughput.

title: Packet transfer and network overhead
subject: Computer Networks
cue: The source label “Network Flow” contains delay, handshaking and packet-overhead questions.
theory: For a link, serialization time is L/R and propagation time is d/v.
Compute header overhead per resulting packet or fragment, then sum; acknowledgements provide feedback about delivery.

recall.q: Does the source label here mean maximum-flow/min-cut algorithms?
recall.a: No. These PYQs concern communication delay, reliability and packetization.

pitfall: Inspect the actual packet sizes and header definitions rather than applying graph maximum-flow formulas.

correction.original: The PYQ topic label is Network Flow.
correction.corrected: Use Packet transfer and network overhead for these PYQs.
correction.reason: The displayed questions concern handshake reliability, propagation/transmission time and fragmentation overhead, not maximum-flow algorithms.

title: Network-layer forwarding
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Route packets between networks with logical addresses.
theory: IP forwarding chooses a next hop from a routing table; CIDR forwarding uses the longest matching prefix.
Routing computes or learns routes; forwarding applies them to individual packets.

recall.q: Which route wins when both /16 and /24 match?
recall.a: The /24 route.

pitfall: Longest prefix is evaluated before considering a less-specific route's metric.

title: Protocol roles and encapsulation
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Match protocols to layers or trace a protocol stack.
theory: Each layer supplies a service while communicating logically with peer-layer entities.
Encapsulation adds headers, and sometimes trailers, as data descends the stack.

recall.q: Do TCP acknowledgements acknowledge Ethernet frames?
recall.a: No; TCP acknowledges bytes in its transport-level sequence space.

pitfall: Different layers can each implement addressing, reliability or flow control for different scopes.

title: Circuit, packet and virtual-circuit switching
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Compare reserved paths with per-packet sharing.
theory: Circuit switching reserves communication resources for a session; packet switching statistically shares links.
Datagram forwarding treats packets independently; virtual circuits establish forwarding state before data transfer.

recall.q: Can packet switching be connection-oriented?
recall.a: Yes; virtual-circuit packet networks establish a logical connection.

pitfall: Do not equate all packet switching with independent datagram routing.

title: OSI model
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Match layer names with responsibilities.
theory: OSI layers are physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application.
Physical sends signals, link delivers frames over a link, network routes packets, and transport serves application endpoints.

recall.q: Which OSI layer handles routing between networks?
recall.a: Network layer.

pitfall: OSI is a reference model; real protocol stacks do not always implement seven separate components.

title: Independent bit-error probability
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Each of n bits flips independently with probability p.
theory: Probability of an error-free n-bit message is (1−p)ⁿ.
Probability of at least one flipped bit is 1−(1−p)ⁿ.

recall.q: Why multiply the per-bit success probabilities?
recall.a: The bit errors are explicitly independent.

pitfall: np is only an approximation for rare errors, not the exact probability of any error.

title: Pure ALOHA
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Unslotted frame attempts follow a Poisson model.
theory: With normalized offered load G attempts per frame time, pure ALOHA throughput is S=G e^(−2G).
The vulnerable period is two frame times; maximum normalized throughput is 1/(2e) at G=1/2.

recall.q: How do you convert attempts/s into G?
recall.a: Multiply the attempt rate by one frame's transmission time.

pitfall: G includes retransmissions, not just newly generated frames.

title: Routing algorithms
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A topology and costs determine next hops or paths.
theory: Link-state routing distributes topology information and computes shortest paths; distance-vector routing exchanges neighbor estimates.
A spanning tree in bridged LANs prevents forwarding loops, rather than finding every shortest route.

recall.q: Why do bridges use a spanning-tree protocol?
recall.a: To remove forwarding loops while retaining connectivity.

pitfall: A minimum spanning tree and a shortest-path tree solve different optimization problems.

title: Routing protocol behavior
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Classify exchanges or reason about updates.
theory: Routing protocols specify how routers learn, advertise and update reachability information.
Link-state and distance-vector approaches differ in the information shared and computation performed.

recall.q: What does a link-state router need to compute routes?
recall.a: A view of the topology and link costs for its routing scope.

pitfall: A route advertisement is control-plane information, not the application packet itself.

title: Sliding-window protocols
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Sequence bits, window size and retransmission policy are given.
theory: For m-bit sequence numbers, conventional Go-Back-N permits sender window at most 2ᵐ−1 with receiver window 1.
Selective Repeat with equal send/receive windows requires window at most 2^(m−1) to avoid ambiguity.

recall.q: Why must Selective Repeat leave enough sequence space outside its current window?
recall.a: So delayed old frames cannot be mistaken for a new cycle's frames.

pitfall: Window bounds depend on receiver behavior; do not apply Go-Back-N's bound to Selective Repeat.

title: Slotted ALOHA
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Transmissions begin only at aligned slot boundaries.
theory: With Poisson attempts and normalized load G, throughput is S=G e^(−G).
Maximum throughput is 1/e at G=1, because the vulnerable interval is one frame time.

recall.q: Why does slotting improve ALOHA's maximum throughput?
recall.a: It halves the vulnerable period compared with pure ALOHA.

pitfall: Time synchronization is required for the slotted model.

title: Socket API
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Client/server calls create, bind, listen or accept endpoints.
theory: A TCP server normally uses socket, bind, listen and accept; a client uses socket and connect.
accept returns a socket for the accepted connection while the listening socket remains available.

recall.q: Does listen itself return a connected client socket?
recall.a: No; accept does.

pitfall: A UDP connect call sets a peer association; it does not create TCP-style reliability or a handshake.

title: Stop-and-wait ARQ
subject: Computer Networks
cue: The sender must receive an ACK before sending the next frame.
theory: Only one data frame is outstanding; timeout and retransmission recover loss.
With no loss and negligible ACK size, cycle time is frame-transmission time plus round-trip propagation.

recall.q: What limits stop-and-wait throughput on a long link?
recall.a: Waiting for the acknowledgement while no new data frame can be sent.

pitfall: Include ACK transmission or processing when the question says it is non-negligible.

title: Subnetting and longest-prefix match
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Allocate address blocks or choose a route.
theory: A /p IPv4 block has 2^(32−p) addresses and must be aligned to that block size.
For route lookup, choose the most specific matching prefix.

recall.q: Can any arbitrary group of 64 consecutive addresses be one /26 block?
recall.a: No; its start must be aligned to a 64-address boundary.

pitfall: Distinguish total address count from usable host count and state subnet assumptions.

title: TCP reliability and flow control
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Sequence numbers, ACKs, receive windows and data rates appear.
theory: TCP sequence numbers count bytes; a cumulative ACK normally names the next byte expected.
Outstanding data is constrained by min(receiver window, congestion window); rough window-limited rate is usable window/RTT.

recall.q: A segment starts at byte 100 and carries 50 bytes. What ACK follows in order?
recall.a: 150, assuming no missing earlier bytes.

pitfall: SYN and FIN consume sequence numbers; pure ACKs normally do not.

title: Token-bucket traffic shaping
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A rate limit allows a bounded burst.
theory: Tokens accumulate at rate r up to bucket capacity B; transmission consumes tokens proportional to data size.
Over interval t, traffic is bounded by B+rt when starting with a full bucket, subject to any link-rate limit.

recall.q: What allows a token bucket to send faster than r briefly?
recall.a: Previously accumulated tokens.

pitfall: Average token rate and physical peak transmission rate are different limits.

title: UDP
subject: Computer Networks
cue: Datagrams, ports, checksums or connected UDP sockets are discussed.
theory: UDP preserves datagram boundaries and adds ports with minimal transport machinery; it does not itself ensure delivery or ordering.
Its checksum can be omitted in IPv4; in IPv6 it is required by default, with narrowly specified exceptions.

recall.q: Does using UDP prevent IP packets from taking different routes?
recall.a: No. Routing is performed by IP independently of that transport choice.

pitfall: A connected UDP socket still does not provide TCP's handshake, retransmission or byte stream.

correction.original: UDP header checksum is described simply as optional.
correction.corrected: It is optional for IPv4; IPv6 requires it by default, apart from explicitly specified exceptions.
correction.reason: The IP version matters. RFC 8200 section 8.1 states the IPv6 default requirement.

title: Sequence-number wraparound
subject: Computer Networks
cue: A finite counter is consumed at a known rate.
theory: A b-bit sequence space has 2ᵇ distinct values; wrap time = 2ᵇ / values consumed per second.
For TCP, count bytes per second rather than bits per second.

recall.q: At R bits/s, how long to consume a b-bit TCP byte-sequence space?
recall.a: 2ᵇ×8/R seconds under continuous full-rate data transfer.

pitfall: For generated identifiers, deduct host and per-tick counter bits before calculating the clock wrap period.

title: Armstrong's axioms
subject: Databases
cue: Derive a functional dependency from a given set.
theory: Reflexivity: if Y⊆X then X→Y. Augmentation: X→Y implies XZ→YZ. Transitivity: X→Y and Y→Z imply X→Z.
These rules are sound and complete for functional-dependency implication.

recall.q: How can you test whether X→Y follows from F?
recall.a: Compute X⁺ using F and check whether Y⊆X⁺.

pitfall: Do not reverse an FD; X→Y does not imply Y→X.

title: B-trees and B+ trees
subject: Databases
cue: Find fanout, height, splits or block accesses.
theory: A balanced search tree keeps leaves at the same depth; high fanout reduces disk accesses.
In a B+ tree, data entries are at leaves and internal nodes guide search; leaf links support range scans.
If order means maximum m children, a nonroot internal node usually has at least ceil(m/2) children; confirm the question's convention.

recall.q: Why are B+ trees effective for range queries?
recall.a: Linked ordered leaves allow sequential scanning after one search.

pitfall: “Order” and “degree” conventions vary; do not import a formula without matching definitions.

title: Candidate keys
subject: Databases
cue: Find minimal attribute sets that determine the whole relation.
theory: X is a superkey if its closure X⁺ contains all attributes.
It is a candidate key if no proper subset is a superkey.

recall.q: How do you test a proposed candidate key?
recall.a: Check that its closure is all attributes, then check minimality.

pitfall: A key with fewer attributes is not necessarily the only candidate key.

title: Conflict serializability
subject: Databases
cue: Interleaved reads and writes must match a serial order.
theory: Operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes.
Add Ti→Tj when Ti's conflicting operation comes first; the schedule is conflict serializable exactly when the graph is acyclic.
Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, but the converse need not hold.

recall.q: What does a cycle in the precedence graph prove?
recall.a: The schedule is not conflict serializable.

pitfall: A cycle does not by itself disprove view serializability.

correction.original: Conflict serializability is called a weaker condition than view serializability.
correction.corrected: Conflict serializability is stronger: every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable; the converse need not hold.
correction.reason: The source reverses the set inclusion between the two schedule classes.

title: Database design
subject: Databases
cue: Identify entities, dependencies and redundancy.
theory: Start from the facts to represent, their identifiers and relationships.
Translate requirements into schemas and constraints, then check dependency-based redundancy and decomposition properties.

recall.q: Why is choosing a primary key alone insufficient for schema design?
recall.a: Other functional dependencies can still create redundancy and update anomalies.

pitfall: A current data sample can disprove an FD but cannot prove it holds for every valid future instance.

title: Normalization
subject: Databases
cue: Given FDs and keys, decide the highest normal form.
theory: In 3NF, every nontrivial FD X→A must have X a superkey or A prime; BCNF requires X to be a superkey.
A prime attribute belongs to at least one candidate key. Check all candidate keys, not only a chosen primary key.
A suitable 3NF synthesis can preserve dependencies and be lossless; those properties do not follow from arbitrary 3NF component schemas alone.

recall.q: How does BCNF strengthen 3NF?
recall.a: It removes the allowance for a nonkey determinant when the dependent attribute is prime.

pitfall: Do not assume a decomposition is lossless merely because every component is in 3NF or BCNF.

correction.original: 3NF decomposition is stated to be always lossless and dependency preserving.
correction.corrected: A suitable synthesis algorithm guarantees a lossless, dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition; an arbitrary decomposition into 3NF relations need not have these properties.
correction.reason: Existence of a decomposition with guarantees does not make those guarantees automatic for every decomposition.

title: Database schema and instance
subject: Databases
cue: Distinguish structure from current stored data.
theory: A schema defines relation names, attributes, domains and constraints.
An instance is the collection of tuples at a particular time.

recall.q: Does adding a row normally change the schema?
recall.a: No; it changes the instance.

pitfall: Properties of one instance are not automatically constraints of the schema.

title: Lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition
subject: Databases
cue: A relation is split into smaller schemas.
theory: For a binary decomposition R into R1 and R2, losslessness under FDs holds when their intersection functionally determines R1 or R2.
Dependency preservation means the projected dependencies together imply the original FDs.

recall.q: What must the shared attributes determine for a binary lossless join?
recall.a: All attributes of at least one component.

pitfall: The binary intersection test cannot be applied unchanged to an arbitrary multiway decomposition.

correction.original: BCNF decomposition is stated to be always lossless.
correction.corrected: The standard decomposition algorithm using a violating dependency is lossless. Arbitrary BCNF components do not themselves guarantee a lossless join.
correction.reason: Losslessness is a property of the decomposition, separate from each component’s normal form.

title: ER diagrams and relational mapping
subject: Databases
cue: Map entities, relationships, participation and cardinality.
theory: Entity sets generally become relations; relationship mapping depends on 1:1, 1:N or M:N cardinality.
An M:N relationship usually needs a separate relation containing participating keys and relationship attributes.

recall.q: Where is the foreign key commonly placed for a 1:N relationship?
recall.a: On the N side, referring to the 1-side entity.

pitfall: Total participation and maximum cardinality express different constraints.

title: Functional dependencies
subject: Databases
cue: Equal determinant values force equal dependent values.
theory: X→Y means any two valid tuples agreeing on X must also agree on Y.
To compute X⁺, repeatedly add RHS attributes whose LHS is already in the closure.

recall.q: What does X⁺ contain?
recall.a: All attributes functionally determined by X under the given dependencies.

pitfall: An FD is a rule across tuples, not a function from each row position to another.

title: Indexing and file organization
subject: Databases
cue: Estimate lookup I/O or classify dense, sparse and secondary indexes.
theory: A dense index has entries for every search-key value or record as defined; a sparse index omits some entries and normally relies on ordered data.
Multilevel indexing reduces lookup depth by indexing the index.

recall.q: Why does sparse indexing usually require the data file to be ordered on the search key?
recall.a: An index entry identifies where to begin a local ordered scan.

pitfall: Index height, data-page access and cached root access may be counted separately.

title: Joins and join cardinality
subject: Databases
cue: Combine matching rows from two relations.
theory: An inner theta join keeps pairs satisfying its predicate; an outer join also preserves unmatched rows from the specified side with NULL padding.
For a particular matching key value, a rows on one side and b on the other produce a×b matching pairs.

recall.q: If three rows and four rows share one join key, how many pairs result?

pitfall: Matching key values can repeat; do not assume one output tuple per input tuple without a uniqueness constraint.

title: Multivalued dependencies and 4NF
subject: Databases
cue: Two independent sets of values depend on the same determinant.
theory: X↠Y expresses an independent multivalued fact for fixed X.
4NF requires every nontrivial multivalued dependency to have a superkey determinant.

recall.q: Why can a BCNF relation still have redundancy?
recall.a: Independent multivalued facts may cause repeated combinations even without a violating FD.

pitfall: An MVD is not merely an FD with several attributes on its RHS.

title: Natural join
subject: Databases
cue: Tables share attribute names and a join has no explicit predicate.
theory: Natural join equates all equally named attributes and includes one copy of each shared attribute.
With no shared attributes, natural join becomes a Cartesian product under the usual relational definition.

recall.q: Which columns does natural join match?
recall.a: Every attribute name common to both input schemas.

pitfall: An unintended shared column name changes the join condition.

title: Normal-form tests
subject: Databases
cue: Check 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF conditions.
theory: 2NF disallows partial dependence of a nonprime attribute on a proper subset of a candidate key.
3NF and BCNF are checked against nontrivial implied FDs, using prime attributes and superkeys.

recall.q: Can a relation with a single-attribute candidate key still violate 3NF?
recall.a: Yes; a nonkey determinant can create a violating dependency.

pitfall: No partial dependency does not mean there are no transitive-dependency problems.

title: Query interpretation
subject: Databases
cue: Translate an English condition into relational operations.
theory: Selection filters rows, projection selects attributes, and joins combine facts.
“For every” often suggests division or a NOT EXISTS counterexample pattern.

recall.q: How can “all required items are present” be expressed logically?
recall.a: There does not exist a required item that is missing.

pitfall: “Some” and “every” lead to different queries; test a tiny counterexample dataset.

title: Referential integrity
subject: Databases
cue: Foreign-key changes must preserve valid references.
theory: A non-NULL foreign-key value must match a referenced key, subject to the schema's declared matching rules.
Deletes and updates may be rejected, cascaded or set to NULL according to the declared action.

recall.q: Must a foreign-key column itself be unique?
recall.a: No, unless an additional uniqueness constraint says so.

pitfall: Foreign keys can be nullable; do not assume NOT NULL without a declaration.

title: Relational algebra
subject: Databases
cue: Trace selection, projection, union, difference and division.
theory: Classical relational algebra uses sets, so projection eliminates duplicate tuples.
Union and difference require compatible schemas; selection and projection have different roles.

recall.q: What is the difference between σ and π?
recall.a: σ filters tuples by a predicate; π keeps chosen attributes.

pitfall: SQL normally uses bag semantics, so direct translation may require DISTINCT.

title: Relational calculus
subject: Databases
cue: A logical formula describes the desired result.
theory: Relational calculus is declarative: it states which tuples satisfy a condition.
Tuple calculus variables denote tuples; domain calculus variables denote individual attribute values.

recall.q: What does calculus specify that algebra expresses operationally?
recall.a: The property of the answer, rather than a sequence of relational operators.

pitfall: Unrestricted negation can describe values outside the stored database domain.

title: Relational model
subject: Databases
cue: Reason about attributes, tuples, domains and keys.
theory: A relation is a set of tuples over named attributes and domains in the mathematical model.
Tuple order and attribute-display order do not define relation meaning.

recall.q: Does the relational model assign a meaningful first row?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Database tables may permit duplicates unless constrained; distinguish SQL behavior from the mathematical model.

title: SQL and NULL semantics
subject: Databases
cue: Evaluate SELECT, GROUP BY, aggregates or subqueries.
theory: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(expression) ignores NULL expressions; ordinary comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN.
SELECT keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT is requested.

recall.q: Why can NOT IN behave unexpectedly if its subquery contains NULL?
recall.a: A comparison may become UNKNOWN, so the row fails the WHERE filter.

pitfall: Use IS NULL for NULL tests; x = NULL is not the intended test.

title: Safe and domain-independent queries
subject: Databases
cue: A calculus expression might produce infinitely many outside values.
theory: A safe query restricts answers to a finite, database-relevant domain using appropriate range restrictions.
Unrestricted “all values not in R” can range beyond values appearing in the database.

recall.q: Why is {x : x is not in R} unsafe over an unbounded domain?
recall.a: It can return infinitely many unrelated values.

pitfall: Finite output on one particular instance does not alone establish general safety.

title: Superkeys
subject: Databases
cue: An attribute set determines every attribute.
theory: A superkey may contain unnecessary attributes; a candidate key is a minimal superkey.
Any superset of a superkey is also a superkey.

recall.q: Is every superkey a candidate key?
recall.a: No; it may fail minimality.

pitfall: Minimal means no proper subset works, not globally smallest cardinality.

title: Timestamp ordering
subject: Databases
cue: Operations are checked against read/write timestamps.
theory: Basic timestamp ordering enforces an order based on transaction timestamps.
A write by T is rejected if TS(T) is older than a conflicting recorded read or write timestamp; Thomas's write rule changes treatment of obsolete writes.

recall.q: Can you use Thomas's write rule in every timestamp-ordering question?
recall.a: No; use it only when specified.

pitfall: Basic timestamp ordering and Thomas's write rule accept different schedules.

title: Transactions, recovery and schedules
subject: Databases
cue: Analyze commits, dirty reads and concurrent operations.
theory: ACID denotes atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.
Recoverable schedules commit a reader only after the writer it read from commits; cascadeless schedules read only committed data; strict schedules also avoid overwriting uncommitted writes.

recall.q: Does conflict serializability alone guarantee recoverability?
recall.a: No; commit/read dependencies must also be checked.

pitfall: Serialization order and commit order are different constraints.

title: Tuple relational calculus
subject: Databases
cue: Tuple variables and existential or universal quantifiers appear.
theory: TRC binds variables to tuples and checks their attributes against predicates.
An existential condition needs one witness; a universal condition needs every allowed witness to satisfy it.

recall.q: How can ∀x P(x) be rewritten using existential quantification?

pitfall: Keep variable scopes explicit; a quantifier only binds occurrences inside its scope.

title: Two-phase locking
subject: Databases
cue: A schedule acquires and releases locks.
theory: In 2PL, a growing phase acquires locks and a shrinking phase releases them; after the first unlock, no new lock is acquired.
2PL guarantees conflict serializability but may deadlock. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit or abort.

recall.q: Does basic 2PL prevent deadlock?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Strict 2PL and rigorous 2PL differ: rigorous holds both shared and exclusive locks to the end.

title: Adders
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Find sum, carry or delay of an adder circuit.
theory: A half adder gives S=A⊕B and C=AB.
A full adder gives S=A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout=AB+ACin+BCin, where + means OR.

recall.q: How many input bits does a full adder combine?
recall.a: Three: A, B and carry-in.

pitfall: Boolean OR in a logic equation is not ordinary arithmetic addition.

title: Array multipliers
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Partial products are arranged in an arithmetic circuit.
theory: Unsigned multiplication forms shifted partial products using AND gates, then adds them.
Two n-bit unsigned operands can require a 2n-bit product.

recall.q: Why do partial-product rows shift left?
recall.a: Each multiplier bit has a different power-of-two weight.

pitfall: Signed multiplication needs sign handling; an unsigned array cannot be used blindly for two's-complement inputs.

title: Binary codes
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Convert between binary, BCD and Gray-code representations.
theory: BCD encodes each decimal digit separately with four bits.
Reflected binary Gray code changes only one bit between consecutive code words; binary-to-Gray is b XOR (b shifted right by 1).

recall.q: Is decimal 12 in BCD the same bit pattern as ordinary binary 12?
recall.a: No: BCD is 0001 0010; ordinary binary is 1100.

pitfall: Not all 4-bit patterns represent valid BCD digits.

title: Boolean algebra
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Simplify expressions without enumerating every input.
theory: Useful identities include X+XY=X, X(X+Y)=X and De Morgan: ¬(XY)=¬X+¬Y.
Use the consensus identity XY+¬XZ+YZ=XY+¬XZ when simplifying a functional expression.

recall.q: What is X+X̅Y equivalent to?
recall.a: X+Y.

pitfall: Removing a logically redundant term can change a circuit's hazard behavior.

title: Booth's multiplication
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Signed binary multiplication inspects neighboring multiplier bits.
theory: In radix-2 Booth recoding, multiplier pairs 01 and 10 trigger opposite add/subtract actions; 00 and 11 trigger neither, followed by arithmetic shifting.
A run of ones can be represented as the difference of two powers of two.

recall.q: Why can Booth recoding reduce work for a long run of 1s?
recall.a: It replaces repeated additions with an add and a subtract at run boundaries.

pitfall: Pair order and the add/subtract convention must match the algorithm given in the question.

title: Canonical SOP and POS
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A function is specified by minterm or maxterm indices.
theory: Canonical SOP is the OR of minterms where F=1; canonical POS is the AND of maxterms where F=0.
Each canonical term contains every variable once, complemented or uncomplemented.

recall.q: Which truth-table rows determine the maxterm indices in canonical POS?
recall.a: Rows where the function equals 0.

pitfall: The maxterm bit-to-literal convention is opposite to the minterm convention.

title: Carry generation and lookahead
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A carry chain determines adder delay.
theory: With Gi=AiBi and Pi=Ai⊕Bi, Ci+1=Gi+PiCi.
Expanding the recurrence lets carry-lookahead logic compute later carries without waiting for every intermediate full adder.

recall.q: What does Gi=1 mean?
recall.a: Bit position i generates a carry regardless of its incoming carry.

pitfall: Some texts define propagate using OR instead of XOR; use one convention consistently.

title: Circuit output tracing
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A network of gates must be evaluated or identified.
theory: Label intermediate wires and write their Boolean functions before simplifying.
For multi-level circuits, preserve every inversion bubble and signal connection.

recall.q: How should you begin a tangled logic-circuit question?
recall.a: Assign names to internal nodes and derive their functions in signal-flow order.

pitfall: Crossing wires are connected only when the diagram marks a junction.

title: Combinational circuit design
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Current inputs alone determine an output.
theory: Build a truth table, simplify each output and implement it with available components.
Multiplexers, decoders, comparators and adders are common combinational building blocks.

recall.q: What distinguishes a combinational circuit from a sequential one?
recall.a: Its output does not depend on stored past state.

pitfall: Propagation delay does not by itself make a circuit sequential.

title: Conjunctive normal form
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A Boolean expression is an AND of OR-clauses.
theory: CNF is a product of sums; clauses need not contain every variable.
Canonical POS is the special form in which each clause is a maxterm containing every variable.

recall.q: Is every CNF expression canonical POS?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Do not expand all missing variables unless a canonical representation is required.

title: Decoders
subject: Digital Logic
cue: n select bits choose one of up to 2ⁿ outputs.
theory: An n-to-2ⁿ decoder activates the output indexed by the input, subject to enables and output polarity.
Combining decoder outputs realizes Boolean functions from their minterms.

recall.q: How many select inputs does a 3-to-8 decoder have?
recall.a: 3, plus any separate enable inputs.

pitfall: Active-low outputs require different combining gates from active-high outputs.

title: Digital-circuit analysis
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Interpret gates, logic levels and component connections.
theory: Separate Boolean functionality from timing constraints.
Check whether outputs are active-high or active-low and whether feedback creates stored state.

recall.q: Can two circuits have the same truth table but different delay?
recall.a: Yes.

pitfall: A functionally correct expression does not establish the timing behavior of its physical implementation.

title: Counters and modulo sequences
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Flip-flops cycle through a prescribed count sequence.
theory: A modulo-N counter requires at least ceil(log₂N) state bits.
Derive next states for valid and unused states; reset or feedback determines the actual cycle.

recall.q: How many flip-flops are needed at minimum for a modulo-10 counter?

pitfall: Four flip-flops allow 16 states but do not guarantee a modulo-16 count sequence.

title: Duality
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Construct a dual expression or use a dual identity.
theory: The Boolean dual swaps AND with OR and 0 with 1, while leaving literals unchanged.
Every valid Boolean identity has a valid dual identity.

recall.q: Is duality the same as complementing a function?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Do not complement variables while forming the dual unless another operation asks for it.

title: Mealy and Moore machines
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Outputs depend on state and possibly current inputs.
theory: Moore output is a function of current state; Mealy output can depend on both state and current input.
State transitions follow the next-state function on the specified clock event.

recall.q: Which machine may change output when input changes without a state transition?
recall.a: A Mealy machine.

pitfall: Count reachable distinguishable states, not merely the number of drawn output labels.

title: Fixed-point representation
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A binary word has a fixed binary-point location.
theory: With f fractional bits, resolution is 2^(−f); interpret the stored integer and multiply by that scale.
The range depends on total bits and whether the format is unsigned or signed.

recall.q: What is the spacing between adjacent values with 4 fractional bits?

pitfall: Adding fractional bits improves resolution but reduces integer range for fixed total width.

title: Flip-flops and excitation
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Given inputs or desired transitions, find the next stored bit.
theory: D flip-flop: Qnext=D. T flip-flop: Qnext=Q⊕T.
JK uses hold, reset, set and toggle for inputs 00,01,10,11 respectively.

recall.q: What input makes a T flip-flop toggle?

pitfall: A characteristic table gives next state from inputs; an excitation table gives inputs needed for a transition.

title: Floating-point representation
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Numbers have a sign, exponent and significand.
theory: A floating-point value uses a scaled significand; normalized binary values usually have an implicit leading 1.
Spacing grows as the exponent grows, so precision is relative rather than uniform over the full range.

recall.q: Are all consecutive representable floating-point values equally spaced?
recall.a: No; spacing depends on magnitude/exponent.

pitfall: A larger range is not the same as greater precision.

title: Functional completeness
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Determine whether a gate set can express every Boolean function.
theory: NAND alone and NOR alone are functionally complete; each can implement NOT and a complete combination of AND/OR.
To show completeness, construct a known complete set from the available gates.

recall.q: How can NAND implement NOT?
recall.a: Tie its two inputs together: ¬(X·X)=¬X.

pitfall: An associative or symmetric gate is not automatically functionally complete.

title: IEEE binary floating point
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Decode sign, biased exponent and fraction fields.
theory: For a normal IEEE binary value, value=(−1)ˢ×(1.f)₂×2^(E−bias).
All-zero exponent encodes zero/subnormal cases; all-one exponent encodes infinity or NaN depending on the fraction.

recall.q: Is the leading significand bit 1 for a subnormal number?
recall.a: No; subnormals use a leading 0 with the special minimum exponent scale.

pitfall: Do not apply the normal-number formula to every exponent pattern.

title: Karnaugh maps
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Minimize a small Boolean function with neighboring cells.
theory: For SOP, group 1s with optional don't-cares in power-of-two rectangular groups; retain only variables constant within a group.
Rows and columns use Gray order, and opposite edges are adjacent.

recall.q: Can a K-map group wrap around an edge?
recall.a: Yes.

pitfall: Diagonal cells are not adjacent; groups may overlap when useful.

title: Little-endian and big-endian storage
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A multibyte word is placed in byte-addressed memory.
theory: Little-endian stores the least-significant byte at the lowest address; big-endian stores the most-significant byte first.
Endianness changes byte order, not the bit order within each byte.

recall.q: In little-endian storage, which byte of 0x12345678 is at the lowest address?

pitfall: Do not reverse every bit or every hexadecimal digit.

title: Memory decoding and interfacing
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Address bits select chips, banks and locations.
theory: Low-order address bits commonly select a location within a chip; higher bits can feed chip-select decoding.
Parallel chips widen a word, whereas additional banks expand the addressable depth.

recall.q: What does adding chips in parallel normally increase?
recall.a: Data width.

pitfall: Address decoding and data-bus width are separate dimensions.

title: Gate-count minimization
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Implement a function with a constrained gate library.
theory: Simplify the function and exploit shared terms, available complements and gate fan-in.
Translate to the allowed gate types before counting physical gates.

recall.q: Why can two equivalent expressions use different numbers of gates?
recall.a: The target gate library, fan-in and shared intermediates differ.

pitfall: A minimum literal count is not automatically a minimum gate count.

title: Minimum product of sums
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Find a compact AND of OR-terms.
theory: Minimize POS by grouping 0 cells on a K-map; a variable fixed at 0 appears uncomplemented in the corresponding sum term.
Choose enough prime implicates to cover all required zeros.

recall.q: Which K-map values are grouped for POS minimization?
recall.a: Zeros, using don't-cares when helpful.

pitfall: The literal polarity differs from the SOP grouping rule.

title: Minimum sum of products
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Cover all true minterms with few product terms.
theory: SOP is an OR of AND-terms; group 1s to remove changing variables.
Prime implicants are maximal valid groups; select a cover that meets the question's cost criterion.

recall.q: Must every prime implicant appear in a minimum SOP?
recall.a: No; only essential ones are mandatory, and others are selected as needed.

pitfall: Fewest terms and fewest literals are not always the same optimization target.

title: Multiplexers
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Select lines choose one data input or implement a Boolean function.
theory: A 2ⁿ-to-1 MUX has n select inputs; assign selected variables to these lines.
For each select combination, simplify the function in the remaining variables to determine the data input.

recall.q: How many select lines does an 8-to-1 MUX need?

pitfall: Follow the specified select-bit order; swapping it permutes the data inputs.

title: Integer representation and overflow
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Interpret bit patterns or perform signed arithmetic.
theory: An n-bit unsigned value ranges from 0 to 2ⁿ−1; two's complement ranges from −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1)−1.
Two's-complement negation inverts bits and adds 1; sign extension preserves its signed value.
Signed addition overflows when equal-sign operands produce an opposite-sign result.

recall.q: Does a carry-out always mean signed overflow?
recall.a: No; carry-out tests unsigned overflow, while signed overflow uses the sign rule.

pitfall: The same bits represent different numbers under unsigned, sign-magnitude and two's-complement interpretations.

title: Positional number systems
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Convert bases or interpret fractional digits.
theory: A digit at position i has weight baseⁱ; positions right of the point have negative powers.
Repeated division converts integer parts, while repeated multiplication converts fractional parts.

recall.q: What is the weight of the first binary digit after the point?

pitfall: A fraction terminating in decimal need not terminate in binary.

title: Prime implicants and tabular minimization
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Choose which implicants are required in a minimal cover.
theory: A prime implicant cannot be enlarged while remaining an implicant.
It is essential if it covers at least one required minterm covered by no other prime implicant.

Quine–McCluskey (tabular method): combine minterms differing in one bit repeatedly, collect uncombined prime implicants, then use a prime-implicant chart to cover every required minterm. Include don’t-cares while combining, but do not require them to be covered.

recall.q: Must all essential prime implicants be selected?
recall.a: Yes.

pitfall: An implicant can be large without being essential.

title: ROM as a logic implementation
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A memory truth table realizes multiple output functions.
theory: For n address inputs and m output bits, a full ROM stores 2ⁿ words of m bits.
Each address stores the output pattern for that input combination.

recall.q: How many stored bits implement 4 inputs and 3 outputs in a full ROM?
recall.a: 2⁴×3=48 bits.

pitfall: Address pins count input combinations; data pins count output functions.

title: Boolean reduction
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Reduce expressions using identities or truth-table equivalence.
theory: Apply absorption, complementation and De Morgan transformations to remove redundancy.
Check an uncertain reduction on discriminating input assignments before accepting it.

recall.q: How can you quickly disprove a proposed Boolean equivalence?
recall.a: Find one input assignment where the outputs differ.

pitfall: Canceling terms as if they were ordinary arithmetic can invalidate Boolean reasoning.

title: Ripple-counter timing
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A clock transition propagates through several flip-flops.
theory: In a ripple counter, later flip-flops are clocked by earlier outputs, so transitions ripple rather than occur together.
Worst-case settling time accumulates along the longest toggling chain.

recall.q: Why can intermediate counter outputs briefly show the wrong count?
recall.a: Flip-flops have nonzero propagation delays.

pitfall: Read the stable output after settling unless the question asks about transient states.

title: Shift registers
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Stored bits move left or right on clock edges.
theory: A shift register transfers each stored bit to an adjacent position and accepts serial or parallel input according to its mode.
Track the exact shift direction and which end receives the new bit.

recall.q: What distinguishes serial-in from parallel-in loading?
recall.a: One bit enters per shift versus multiple bits loaded simultaneously.

pitfall: A diagram's visual left/right direction may differ from numeric significance; label bit positions.

title: Static hazards
subject: Digital Logic
cue: A function should remain constant while one input changes, but a glitch occurs.
theory: A static-1 hazard is a brief 1→0→1 glitch; a static-0 hazard is a brief 0→1→0 glitch.
In two-level SOP, overlapping adjacent 1 regions with a consensus term can remove a static-1 hazard.

recall.q: Can adding a redundant term improve circuit behavior?
recall.a: Yes; it can cover an unequal-delay transition and remove a hazard.

pitfall: Boolean equivalence alone does not imply hazard-free timing.

title: Synchronous and asynchronous circuits
subject: Digital Logic
cue: Determine when state updates occur.
theory: Synchronous circuits coordinate state changes with a clock event; asynchronous circuits respond through signal timing without a single global clock discipline.
Even synchronous circuits must meet setup, hold and propagation-delay constraints.

recall.q: Does a common clock eliminate all timing constraints?
recall.a: No; setup, hold and combinational-path timing still matter.

pitfall: Synchronous state updates are logically coordinated, not physically instantaneous.

title: Banker's algorithm
subject: Operating System
cue: Given Available, Allocation and Maximum, test safety or a new request.
theory: Need = Maximum − Allocation, computed separately for every resource type.
Set Work = Available. Repeatedly choose an unfinished process with Need ≤ Work componentwise, then add its Allocation back to Work. Finishing all processes proves safety.
For a request, check Request ≤ Need and Request ≤ Available; tentatively grant it, then run the safety test.

recall.q: When a process finishes in the safety test, what gets added to Work?
recall.a: Its current Allocation—not its Maximum or remaining Need. The resources notionally borrowed from Work are returned too, so the net increase is Allocation.

pitfall: An unsafe state is not necessarily already deadlocked; it lacks a guarantee for all declared maximum demands.

title: Best-fit allocation
subject: Operating System
cue: Place successive requests into unequal free memory holes.
theory: Choose the smallest available hole whose size is at least the request size.
When splitting is allowed, replace that hole with its unused remainder. Free adjacent holes may be coalesced only when their addresses are adjacent.
External fragmentation means sufficient total free space exists but no single contiguous hole is large enough.

recall.q: Holes are 100, 250 and 180 KB; a 160 KB request arrives. Which hole and remainder?
recall.a: Choose 180 KB, leaving a 20 KB free hole when splitting is allowed.

pitfall: The name “best fit” describes a local selection rule, not globally optimal future memory utilization.

correction.original: Best Fit is described as minimizing internal fragmentation in a dynamic-hole allocation discussion.
correction.corrected: With exact splitting, the remainder stays outside the allocation as a free hole; the characteristic problem is external fragmentation. Internal waste may arise from alignment or an unsplit allocation.
correction.reason: A free remainder outside an allocated block and unused bytes inside it are different kinds of fragmentation.

title: Context switches
subject: Operating System
cue: Count saved execution states or CPU time lost when execution changes.
theory: A context switch saves the current execution state, such as registers, program counter and stack pointer, and restores another process or thread.
A user-to-kernel mode switch can occur without changing the running process.
If each useful CPU slice lasts q and each following switch costs s, the repeating-slice useful fraction is q/(q+s). Check whether initial/final overhead is counted.

recall.q: Does every system call require a process context switch?
recall.a: No. The same process can enter the kernel, receive service, and return without another process running.

pitfall: Do not count a change in privilege mode as a process switch unless the question says execution changes.

title: DMA and CPU interference
subject: Operating System
cue: A controller transfers data directly to memory, with burst or cycle-stealing timing.
theory: The CPU sets up a DMA operation; the controller performs data movement and commonly notifies the CPU when finished.
Cycle stealing takes individual bus cycles; burst transfer holds the bus for a block. Their interference with CPU memory access differs.
If f transfers occur per second and each steals t seconds of an otherwise required CPU resource, the occupied fraction is f×t under that model.

recall.q: Does DMA mean the CPU never participates in I/O?
recall.a: No. Setup, completion handling and possible bus contention still involve or affect the CPU.

pitfall: Convert bytes, words, bits and transfer cycles before computing CPU slowdown; bus occupancy need not equal instruction slowdown without an explicit model.

title: Deadlock strategies
subject: Operating System
cue: Identify prevention, avoidance, or detection from a resource policy.
theory: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait in the usual reusable-resource model.
Prevention rules out a necessary condition; avoidance checks whether a tentative allocation remains safe; detection finds an existing deadlock and requires recovery.
A global resource order breaks circular wait. Requesting everything before holding anything breaks hold-and-wait.

recall.q: Which condition does requesting resources in increasing resource-number order break?
recall.a: Circular wait: a cycle would require the resource order to increase and eventually return to its starting point.

pitfall: A detector uses current outstanding requests; a safety test uses possible remaining maximum needs.

title: Demand paging
subject: Operating System
cue: A page fault probability is combined with much larger disk service time.
theory: With demand paging, a referenced nonresident page must be brought into memory before the access can complete.
If t_fault is the entire faulting-access time, EAT = (1−p)t_hit + p t_fault. If F is only extra fault overhead, EAT = t_hit + pF.
Include a dirty victim’s write-back cost when specified; even a small fault rate can dominate the average.

recall.q: Why can a tiny page-fault rate cause a large slowdown?
recall.a: The fault-service time can be many orders of magnitude larger than a normal memory access.

pitfall: Use one definition of fault time throughout; do not count the retried memory access twice.

title: Disk geometry and access time
subject: Operating System
cue: Convert RPM, sector layout and transfer size into access time.
theory: One revolution takes 60/RPM seconds. With a uniformly random rotational position, average rotational latency is 30/RPM seconds.
Access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time, plus any stated controller or queueing overhead.
Transfer time = data size / transfer rate. Tracks at the same radius across recording surfaces form a cylinder.

recall.q: At 6000 RPM, what are revolution time and average rotational latency?
recall.a: 6000/60 = 100 revolutions/s; one revolution is 10 ms, so average rotational latency is 5 ms.

pitfall: Average latency is half a revolution only under the random-position assumption; a known sector position needs its actual angular distance.

title: Disk scheduling
subject: Operating System
cue: Trace head movement from an initial track and direction.
theory: Total movement is the sum of absolute differences between consecutive head positions, including the initial position.
SSTF picks the currently nearest request. SCAN goes to a physical end before reversing; LOOK reverses at the last pending request.
C-SCAN and C-LOOK service in one direction. Count their return movement if the question’s cost model includes it.

recall.q: What distinguishes LOOK from SCAN?
recall.a: LOOK reverses at the furthest pending request in the current direction; SCAN continues to the physical end.

pitfall: SSTF is greedy, can starve distant requests, and does not guarantee the minimum total movement for every request set.

correction.original: The source says SSTF is optimal for average seek time.
correction.corrected: SSTF minimizes the next seek, not necessarily total or average seek distance over all requests.
correction.reason: Counterexample with distance-proportional seek cost: from track 50, requests {49,52,1} give SSTF path 50→49→52→1, distance 55; path 50→52→49→1 has distance 53.

title: File systems and block addressing
subject: Operating System
cue: Count disk blocks, inode pointers, or levels of indirect addressing.
theory: Contiguous allocation supports direct access but complicates growth; linked allocation follows block pointers; indexed allocation locates blocks through an index.
If a block holds B bytes and each pointer takes p bytes, one index block holds floor(B/p) pointers.
With d direct pointers and one each of single, double and triple indirect pointers, addressable file data is B(d+k+k²+k³), where k=floor(B/p), subject to any other file-size limits.

recall.q: Does an indirect index block store file data in the standard inode model?
recall.a: No. It stores pointers; include it in metadata/storage or I/O counts when asked, but not in the file’s data capacity.

pitfall: Distinguish maximum addressable file bytes from total allocated space including index blocks.

title: fork() and process counting
subject: Operating System
cue: Trace parent/child branches or count output after fork calls.
theory: A successful fork returns 0 in the child and the child PID in the parent; failure returns −1 in the parent without creating a child.
For n unconditional sequential successful forks executed by every live process, total processes = 2ⁿ and newly created children = 2ⁿ−1.
Parent and child normally have separate address spaces. Inherited file descriptors may refer to the same open-file description, so file offsets can be shared.

recall.q: Three unconditional successful fork calls give how many total and newly created processes?
recall.a: 8 total processes and 7 newly created children, if every process reaches all three calls.

pitfall: Conditional branches, short-circuit operators, exits and failures invalidate blindly applying 2ⁿ.

title: I/O handling mechanisms
subject: Operating System
cue: Compare polling, interrupts, DMA, buffering or interrupt-event order.
theory: Polling repeatedly reads device status; interrupt-driven I/O lets the device signal an event; DMA moves data without the CPU copying each item.
A typical interrupt sequence completes the current instruction, saves required state, selects the handler, services the event, and restores state.
Buffering absorbs producer/consumer rate differences; spooling queues jobs for a shared device.

recall.q: Why does interrupt-driven I/O reduce busy waiting?
