recall.a: The CPU can do other work instead of repeatedly checking whether the device is ready.

pitfall: Follow the specified hardware model: vectored interrupt selection and DMA transfer modes have different overheads.

title: I/O and process-state transitions
subject: Operating System
cue: Count ready-queue entries caused by blocking I/O.
theory: A blocking I/O request normally changes a process from running to blocked. Completion changes it from blocked to ready.
The scheduler later changes ready to running; I/O completion does not itself guarantee immediate CPU execution.
Count actual I/O operations and the transitions specified by the question; do not count the initial admission if explicitly excluded.

recall.q: A process makes one blocking read followed by 20 blocking writes; how many I/O-completion entries to ready occur?
recall.a: 21, assuming every operation blocks and each completion makes the process ready once.

pitfall: Running→blocked is not an entry into the ready queue.

title: IPC, pipes and I/O redirection
subject: Operating System
cue: Identify how processes exchange data or redirect standard streams.
theory: Shared-memory IPC exchanges data through a mapped region and still needs synchronization for shared updates.
Message passing exchanges explicit messages; pipes carry streams between file descriptors; sockets can connect local or remote processes.
I/O redirection changes the source/destination associated with a program’s input/output descriptor; it does not require renaming a file.

recall.q: What does using an existing file as a program’s standard input require conceptually?
recall.a: Redirect its standard-input descriptor to that file; the program can keep reading from standard input.

pitfall: Communication and synchronization are related but different: a shared buffer alone does not prevent races.

title: Interrupts and traps
subject: Operating System
cue: Decide what an interrupt changes or compute handler overhead.
theory: Hardware interrupts are triggered by events outside the current instruction; synchronous exceptions/traps arise from instruction execution.
The processor preserves the required state before handling an event. The OS may resume the interrupted process or schedule another.
If r nonoverlapping interrupts occur per second and each costs t seconds, handler-time fraction = rt in that model.

recall.q: Must an interrupt cause a different process to run?
recall.a: No. After handling it, execution may return to the same process; a scheduling decision depends on the event and OS state.

pitfall: Do not equate interrupt entry with a mandatory process context switch.

title: LRU and reference locality
subject: Operating System
cue: An array traversal or reference string asks for LRU page faults.
theory: LRU evicts the resident page whose most recent use is furthest in the past; every hit updates recency.
For C row-major arrays, linear element index of A[i][j] is i×columns+j. Convert byte addresses to page numbers before tracing references.
With f frames, a previously used page misses if at least f distinct other pages have been referenced since its last use.

recall.q: Does a hit change an LRU queue?
recall.a: Yes. The referenced page becomes most recently used even though no page is loaded.

pitfall: Traversing columns of a row-major array can defeat locality; count distinct pages, not just loop iterations.

title: Linked file allocation
subject: Operating System
cue: Each file block reserves bytes for a next-block pointer.
theory: For block size B and pointer size p, payload per block is B−p when the pointer is stored inside every block.
A file of F bytes needs ceil(F/(B−p)) blocks. Unused payload in the final block is n(B−p)−F.
Pointer overhead is np bytes and is separate from unused payload; traversing links makes random access expensive.

recall.q: B=1024 bytes, p=4, F=2041: how many blocks are required?
recall.a: Payload is 1020 bytes per block; ceil(2041/1020)=3 blocks. Unused payload is 3060−2041=1019 bytes.

pitfall: The last block may still reserve a NULL-pointer field; do not silently give it B usable data bytes.

title: Memory allocation and working sets
subject: Operating System
cue: Compare paging/segmentation, fit strategies, or recently used page sets.
theory: Paging maps fixed-size virtual pages to frames; segmentation maps variable-size logical regions and needs bounds checks.
Fixed-size allocation may leave unused space inside an allocation; variable-size contiguous allocation can leave separated external holes.
The working set for a reference window is the set of distinct pages referenced inside that window; update it as old references leave.

recall.q: Can a process fail to obtain 100 KB when total free memory is 150 KB?
recall.a: Yes, with contiguous allocation if no single free hole is at least 100 KB.

pitfall: A working-set window counts recent references or time as specified; it is not simply a fixed number of resident frames.

title: Multilevel page tables
subject: Operating System
cue: Split a virtual address into page-table indices and a page offset.
theory: For byte-addressable memory and page size B=2ᵇ bytes, the low b virtual-address bits are the page offset.
If one table page holds B/p entries of p bytes, an index into that page needs log₂(B/p) bits when that count is a power of two.
Without a TLB or other caching, an L-level page-table walk plus the data access takes L+1 memory accesses, assuming all pages are resident.

recall.q: A 4 KB page-table page with 8-byte entries holds how many entries and index bits?
recall.a: 4096/8=512 entries, requiring 9 index bits.

pitfall: Use virtual address bits to size the table hierarchy; frame-number bits are determined by physical memory.

title: Protection and privileged execution
subject: Operating System
cue: Separate user-mode operations from kernel-controlled resource access.
theory: Hardware privilege levels and memory-access checks keep user code from directly performing protected operations.
A system-call instruction transfers control through a controlled kernel entry point; the kernel validates requested operations.
An access-control matrix associates subjects/domains with objects and rights; ACLs organize rights by object, capabilities by holder/domain.

recall.q: Why is merely hiding an OS function name insufficient protection?
recall.a: A user could still attempt the underlying operation; hardware-enforced privilege and access checks must prevent it.

pitfall: A mode bit alone is useful only when privileged instructions and memory accesses actually enforce it.

title: Page-replacement algorithms
subject: Operating System
cue: Trace FIFO, LRU, OPT or Clock on a page-reference sequence.
theory: FIFO evicts the page loaded earliest; a hit does not change its load order. LRU uses last-reference order, updated on hits.
OPT evicts the page used furthest in the future and gives a minimum fault count for the specified trace and frame count.
Count compulsory first loads as faults. FIFO can show Belady’s anomaly; LRU and OPT have the stack property and do not.

recall.q: If adding a frame increases page faults, can the policy be exact LRU?
recall.a: No. Exact LRU is a stack algorithm, so more frames cannot increase its faults on the same trace.

pitfall: Convert addresses to page numbers first; several consecutive addresses may belong to the same page.

title: Task precedence and parallelism
subject: Operating System
cue: A DAG specifies tasks that must finish before other tasks begin.
theory: An edge A→B means A must finish before B starts. A topological ordering gives a valid serial execution order.
Tasks with no dependency path between them may overlap if resources allow.
With unlimited processors and stated task durations, minimum completion time is the longest weighted path through the dependency DAG.

recall.q: How do you enforce that C starts only after both A and B finish?
recall.a: Make C wait for completion signals from both A and B, or join both tasks before starting C.

pitfall: The FORK/JOIN constructs in a precedence-graph question need not have the same meaning as Unix fork().

title: Processes and states
subject: Operating System
cue: Identify ready, running, blocked and their transitions.
theory: A process is an executing program with an address space, execution state and OS-managed resources.
Ready means eligible to run but waiting for CPU time; blocked means waiting for an event or resource.
Preemption changes running→ready; a blocking request changes running→blocked; event completion changes blocked→ready.

recall.q: What is the difference between ready and blocked?
recall.a: A ready process could execute if assigned a CPU; a blocked process must first wait for its event or resource.

pitfall: Having a program loaded does not mean it is running or even ready.

title: CPU scheduling and metrics
subject: Operating System
cue: Given arrival and burst times, construct a Gantt chart and averages.
theory: Turnaround = completion−arrival. Response = first CPU start−arrival.
For the standard single-CPU-burst model with no I/O, waiting = turnaround−burst. With I/O, exclude blocked time as well when computing ready-queue waiting.
FCFS chooses arrival order; nonpreemptive SJF chooses the shortest ready job at dispatch; priority scheduling follows the stated priority convention.

recall.q: A job arrives at 2, first runs at 5, finishes at 12, and uses 4 CPU units with no I/O. Its response, turnaround and waiting?
recall.a: Response 3, turnaround 10, waiting 6.

pitfall: Do not schedule a short job before it has arrived; “smaller priority number” is not universally higher priority.

title: Critical sections and synchronization
subject: Operating System
cue: Check interleavings, mutual exclusion, progress or bounded waiting.
theory: A race condition occurs when an uncoordinated interleaving of shared operations changes the result; x++ usually includes a read and a write.
A critical-section solution is assessed for mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting, not just one property.
Atomic primitives protect synchronization state. Blocking while holding a lock needed by the waker can cause deadlock.

recall.q: Can a solution satisfy mutual exclusion yet still be incorrect?
recall.a: Yes. It may deadlock, violate progress, or starve a process and violate bounded waiting.

pitfall: A final value from one convenient execution is not proof; examine all relevant interleavings or establish an invariant.

title: Resource-allocation bounds
subject: Operating System
cue: Find a safe order or minimum count of identical resources to prevent deadlock.
theory: Track held resources, outstanding requests and available instances separately.
If n processes each need at most k identical units, acquire them one at a time, and release all upon completion, n(k−1)+1 units guarantee that some process can finish.
The bound comes from the worst stalled arrangement: every process holds k−1 units; one additional unit lets one finish and release its resources.

recall.q: Under that model, three processes each need at most four identical units. What count guarantees freedom from deadlock?

pitfall: The formula is not a substitute for Banker’s algorithm with multiple resource types, different policies or different release assumptions.

title: Resource-allocation graphs
subject: Operating System
cue: A graph contains process/resource nodes and directed request/assignment edges.
theory: A request edge runs process→resource type; an assignment edge runs resource instance→process.
With one instance of every resource type, a cycle is sufficient and necessary for deadlock in the usual resource model.
With multiple instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient: another available instance or a finishing process may break the wait.

recall.q: A multi-instance resource graph has a cycle. What can you conclude?
recall.a: Deadlock is possible, but the cycle alone does not prove it; inspect available instances and possible completions.

pitfall: Reverse request and assignment arrows and the interpretation of the entire graph changes.

title: Round-robin scheduling
subject: Operating System
cue: Each ready process runs for at most a fixed time quantum.
theory: Run the front ready process for min(quantum, remaining burst); if unfinished, append it to the queue after handling arrivals as specified.
A very large quantum approaches FCFS in the standard single-burst model; a very small quantum increases switch overhead.
Compute response from the first slice only, and waiting from all intervals spent ready.

recall.q: If a job has 2 units left and quantum is 5, how long is its next slice?
recall.a: 2 units; it completes without consuming a full 5-unit quantum.

pitfall: Resolve simultaneous arrivals and quantum expiry using the question’s stated queue convention, not an unstated assumption.

title: Semaphores and ordering
subject: Operating System
cue: Choose initial semaphore values and locations of wait/signal.
theory: wait acquires a permit or waits; signal releases a permit. The checking and state change must be atomic with respect to competing operations.
A semaphore initialized to 1 can guard a critical section. Initialized to 0, it can make one activity wait for another’s completion signal.
For a bounded buffer of size N, empty=N, full=0 and a mutex=1 are typical initial values; obtain availability before holding the buffer mutex.

recall.q: To force B after A, how should a completion semaphore start and be used?
recall.a: Start S=0. A performs its work then signal(S); B does wait(S) before its work.

pitfall: Do not treat the source’s while-test and decrement pseudocode as ordinary independently interleavable C statements; the semaphore operation must be correctly synchronized.

title: Shortest remaining time first
subject: Operating System
cue: New jobs may preempt a running job based on remaining CPU time.
theory: SRTF selects the ready job with the least remaining processing time and reevaluates when arrivals or completions change the ready set.
Before comparing at a new arrival, subtract the CPU time already consumed by the current job.
Its ideal optimality assumes known processing times, permitted preemption and no preemption cost; repeated short arrivals can starve a long job.

recall.q: A job started with burst 8 and has run for 5; a burst-4 job arrives. Must it preempt?
recall.a: No. The current job has 3 left, which is shorter than 4.

pitfall: Compare remaining time, not the current job’s original burst.

title: System calls and kernel entry
subject: Operating System
cue: Distinguish library functions, traps and OS services.
theory: A system call requests a kernel service through a controlled user-to-kernel transition.
A library routine may make zero, one or multiple system calls; its name alone does not imply a kernel entry on every use.
exec replaces the calling process’s program image; fork creates a new process; wait waits for a child-state event.

recall.q: Does a successful exec create a second process?
recall.a: No. It replaces the current process’s program image; process creation is a separate operation such as fork.

pitfall: Do not assume a successful exec returns to the old program’s next instruction.

title: Threads and execution models
subject: Operating System
cue: Decide which state is shared and how user threads map to kernel threads.
theory: Threads in one process normally share code, global data, heap and open-file resources; each has its own registers, program counter and stack.
In a many-to-one user-thread model, a blocking kernel call can block the single kernel scheduling entity, preventing the other user threads from running.
With multiple kernel threads, another runnable thread may continue. Shared data still needs synchronization.

recall.q: Which is private to each thread: heap, global variables, registers or open files?
recall.a: Registers, including the program counter; the thread also has its own stack. The other listed resources are normally shared within a process.

pitfall: The “one blocked thread blocks them all” claim depends on the user-to-kernel thread mapping, not simply on the phrase user-level thread.

title: TLB and effective access time
subject: Operating System
cue: Combine translation-cache hit ratio with page-table walk costs.
theory: A TLB caches virtual-page translations; a miss normally requires a page-table walk, not necessarily a page fault.
For a serial TLB lookup time t, memory time m, hit ratio h and resident L-level tables: EAT = h(t+m)+(1−h)(t+(L+1)m), ignoring other caches.
Page offset bits are unchanged during translation; replace the virtual page number with the physical frame number.

recall.q: Does a TLB miss imply that the requested page is absent from RAM?
recall.a: No. The translation may be absent from the TLB while the page is resident; a page-table walk can find it.

pitfall: Use the timing model given: parallel lookup, cached page-table entries or page faults change the simple serial formula.

title: Virtual addresses and paging
subject: Operating System
cue: Find page numbers, offsets, frame numbers or page-table sizes.
theory: For byte address A and page size B: virtual page number = floor(A/B), offset = A mod B.
If the page maps to frame f, physical address = fB+offset. A v-bit virtual address and 2ᵇ-byte pages give 2ᵛ⁻ᵇ virtual pages.
A flat page table has one entry per virtual page in the modeled address space; physical frame count instead determines frame-number width.

recall.q: Address 9000 with 4096-byte pages: what are page number and offset?
recall.a: Page number 2 and offset 808, because 9000=2×4096+808.

pitfall: Page-table size depends on virtual address space and entry size, not simply the amount of physical RAM.
